## The idea

Play C, E, and G together. Remove E and the chord loses the property that tells
you whether it is major or minor. Remove G and the sound loses much of its
weight. Three notes are enough to establish a compact harmonic identity.

A *triad* contains a root and two notes stacked a third apart. Count semitones
instead of letter names for now. A major third spans four semitones and a minor
third spans three. Stack them as 4 then 3 for a major triad, 3 then 4 for minor,
3 then 3 for diminished, and 4 then 4 for augmented. The four qualities become
four arrays rather than four diagrams.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 84
use_synth :piano

define :make_triad do |root, thirds|
  [root, root + thirds[0], root + thirds[0] + thirds[1]]
end

define :play_both_ways do |notes|
  play_chord notes, release: 1.2
  sleep 2
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.45
    sleep 0.5
  end
  sleep 1
end

qualities = {
  major: [4, 3],
  minor: [3, 4],
  diminished: [3, 3],
  augmented: [4, 4]
}

qualities.each do |name, thirds|
  triad = make_triad(note(:c4), thirds)
  puts "#{name}: #{triad}"
  play_both_ways triad
end

puts "matches Sonic Pi: #{make_triad(60, [4, 3]) == chord(:c4, :major).to_a}"
```

The major and minor chords differ at their middle note. Diminished compresses
both thirds and sounds pinched. Augmented expands both and withholds a stable
fifth. The block presentation gives the chord as one object; the arpeggio makes
its interval construction easier to follow.

## Change one thing

1. Move the root from `:c4` to `:a3`. The quality remains intact because every
   pitch receives the same offset.
2. Reverse `[4, 3]` while the chord is sounding. One changed ordering turns major
   into minor without moving the root or highest note by much.
3. Change the synth to `:prophet` and use a longer release. Overlap makes the
   arpeggio approach the block chord, while separate attacks remain audible.

## Why it works

The root is the reference address. The first third is an offset from the root,
and the second is an offset from the middle note. Cumulative addition produces
absolute pitches. This is the same pattern used for scales, with three notes and
two larger steps.

The outer interval also changes by quality. Major and minor triads both span a
perfect fifth of seven semitones. Diminished spans six, the tritone from Lesson
19. Augmented spans eight. That outer frame explains why changing one internal
third affects stability as well as colour.

Spelling still carries musical information. C-E-G and C-F-flat-G can collapse
to related piano keys under equal temperament, yet the stacked-third account
depends on letter sequence as well as semitone distance. The constructor in this
lesson deliberately works at the sounding-pitch layer. When these chords enter
a key and a score, keep the spelled root and chord quality beside the generated
integers. That gives later notation code enough information to print the chord
without guessing how its pitches acquired their jobs.

`chord(:c4, :major)` provides a reference for one case. Extend that comparison
to the other qualities before trusting a reusable constructor. Ruby syntax can
confirm that the program parses. Sonic Pi auditioning still has to confirm
balance, timing, and the claimed distinctions.

## Take it further

Build a four-choice chord-quality drill from `qualities`. Start with
`use_random_seed 42`, choose a quality and a root from MIDI 48 through 59, play
the arpeggio followed by the block, wait four beats, then print the answer. Run
ten trials and tally your answers outside the program. Each trial must use the
same synth, rhythm, amplitude, and register span.
